text: On XX/XX/XXXX, I received an email from " XXXX XXXX '' at Zion Debt Holdings, LLC, wherein XXXX XXXX claimed that I had a current balance due of {$2600.00} from a XXXXXXXX XXXX account that " was not properly closed. '' The email provided a link to make the payment with a Zions account number. I assumed this was spam or some kind of phishing scam. On XX/XX/XXXX, I received a text message from an unknown number, claiming to be Zions Debt Holdings. The sender requested that I call their number to " resolve '' my " past due XXXXXXXX XXXX account, '' after which they would " offer to expunge it from the credit agencies. '' After this second communication, I thought it would be prudent to review my credit reports, which I did last night ( XX/XX/XXXX ). Much to my surprise, there was, in fact, a collection account reported to XXXX by Zions Debt Holdings on XX/XX/XXXX. I immediately initiated a dispute of this debt with XXXX. For context, I did have a XXXXXXXX XXXX account from XX/XX/XXXX- XX/XX/XXXX. However, I terminated the account in XX/XX/XXXX because it was created under false pretenses by a former XXXX representative, XXXX XXXX. Moreover, even if this was a legitimate debt ( which it is NOT ), in North Carolina, a debt buyer must initiate collection efforts within 3 years of the last activity on the account. See N.C.G.S. 1-52 ( 1 ), 58-70-115 ( 4 ). In both communications, Zions claimed to have purchased this alleged debt from XXXX ( see attached communications ). Zions, however, reported this alleged debt to XXXX on XX/XX/XXXX, which was more than 3 years after my last activity with XXXX. Zions also waited almost an entire year thereafter to make a collection effort ( which failed to contain the necessary disclosures required under state and federal law ).
